meta.title: Who really said "I have sold more books on physics than Madonna has on sex"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Stephen Hawking did publish this line — but he was quoting someone else. Wikiquote credits the remark to Nathan Myhrvold, and the popular version is a splice.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have sold more books on physics than Madonna has on sex'?
meta.ogDescription: Hawking published the line, but credited it to Nathan Myhrvold. The widely shared first-person version is an unsourced splice of two separate statements.

answer.label: Not Stephen Hawking — actually Nathan Myhrvold
answer.authorDates: Born 1959 · Microsoft’s first chief technology officer; a former postdoctoral researcher under Hawking
answer.sourceLine: Hawking put this sentence in print, but not as his own: in the Foreword to The Illustrated A Brief History of Time he attributes it to Nathan Myhrvold of Microsoft, a former post-doc of his. The version that circulates — a first-person boast opening “All of my life, I have been fascinated by the big questions…” — is recorded by Wikiquote ↗ as an unsourced variant that welds that Foreword remark onto an unrelated sentence from a 1997 television programme.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Illustrated A Brief History of Time
Nathan Myhrvold, then of Microsoft — “a former post-doc of mine”, in Hawking’s words
An unsourced splice of two separate statements

source.excerpt: As Nathan Myhrvold of Microsoft (a former post-doc of mine) remarked: I have sold more books on physics than Madonna has on sex.
trail: Wikiquote’s Stephen Hawking page ↗ carries the real sentence — “All my life, I have been fascinated by the big questions that face us, and have tried to find scientific answers to them” — sourced to the 1997 television programme Stephen Hawking’s Universe.

Directly beneath it, the same entry flags the familiar longer quip as an unsourced variant, and explains that it “seems to combine” that television sentence with a separate statement from the Foreword to The Illustrated A Brief History of Time.

That Foreword statement is the one carrying the Madonna line, and it is framed as a quotation: Hawking credits it to Nathan Myhrvold ↗, Microsoft’s first chief technology officer, who had been a postdoctoral researcher under him at Cambridge.

We were not able to open the Foreword itself: the 1996 edition is on the Internet Archive ↗ but access-restricted, and its search-inside service was unreachable from here. This page therefore rests on Wikiquote’s transcription, and asserts no page number or edition detail beyond what that entry states.
source.excerptNote: The Foreword sentence as Wikiquote ↗ transcribes it. Note the frame: Hawking is reporting a remark, and names the person who made it.

author.heading: About Nathan Myhrvold
author.metaLine: Born 1959 · American technologist, inventor and author
author.bio: Nathan Myhrvold is an American inventor, scientist and businessman who served as the first chief technology officer of Microsoft, and later co-founded Intellectual Ventures and TerraPower. Before that he held a postdoctoral fellowship at Cambridge under Stephen Hawking. He is also the principal author of Modernist Cuisine, a work about food that is, characteristically, mostly about physics.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case. Hawking really did publish the sentence, so a reader who finds it in his book is not imagining things — but he published it as someone else’s line, and the version that spread quietly removed the credit.

items.why: Quote sites print the line in Hawking’s voice with no mention of Myhrvold. Wikiquote ↗ records the popular wording as an unsourced variant rather than a quotation of Hawking.

items.scope: How the popular version was built
items.why: The circulating text opens with a genuine Hawking sentence from the 1997 programme Stephen Hawking’s Universe, then bolts on the Foreword’s Madonna remark with a “Perhaps that is why…” bridge that appears in neither source, per Wikiquote ↗.

Myhrvold ↗ is an inventor and businessman, Microsoft’s former chief technology officer and principal author of Modernist Cuisine — and, earlier, a postdoc of Hawking’s. Hawking names him in the Foreword.

misattribution.truthLine: Hawking wrote it down; Myhrvold said it. The line is a real remark by a real person — just not the person whose name it travels under, as Wikiquote ↗ documents.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: A Brief History of Time did something science books are not supposed to do: it became a genuine mass-market bestseller, and stayed one for years. The joke lands because it measures physics against the most reliable seller in publishing, and physics wins.

It is also a neat illustration of how attribution decays. Nothing was fabricated here — the sentence is real, the book is real, the credit was printed. All that happened is that a quotation frame got dropped somewhere in the retelling, and a joke changed owners.
detailsBody: The mechanism is worth naming, because it is common. When an author quotes someone in their own book, the quotation lives inside that author’s pages. Excerpt it without the frame and the surrounding voice becomes the speaker by default — no bad faith required.

The tell here is the “Perhaps that is why…” bridge in the popular version. It reads smoothly, which is exactly the problem: it is the seam where two separate statements were joined, and it appears in neither of the sources being joined.
context.pull: Nothing was invented. A quotation frame was simply dropped — and the joke changed owners.

Nathan Myhrvold is an American inventor, scientist and businessman, former CTO of Microsoft, co-founder of Intellectual Ventures and TerraPower, principal author of Modernist Cuisine; born 3 August 1959.
The Illustrated A Brief History of Time (1996) is held by the Internet Archive but is access-restricted; its Foreword text could not be read from here.
